articles.headline: Waymo Puts Toronto on the Map for Its Robotaxis
keyFacts: Waymo announced that its autonomous ride service will expand to Canada with a Toronto launch planned for 2028.
Waymo is partnering with Toronto-based Element Fleet Management for vehicle maintenance, validation driving, and customer service.
Human-driven Waymo vehicles will begin mapping streets and testing driving conditions in select Toronto neighborhoods in the coming days.
body: Waymo is bringing its autonomous ride services across the border to Canada for the first time.

The company said in a blog post on Friday that its robotaxis will be available for you to book rides in the app in the Toronto area in 2028. It will start with a limited number of its mainstay Jaguar I-Pace electric SUVs, and will add more over time.

But if you’re in Toronto, you can expect to see Waymo cars, driven by humans, in the coming days as the company maps local street networks and acclimates its autonomous technology to traffic patterns and driving conditions.

Waymo will test in select Toronto neighborhoods, including Liberty Village, St. Lawrence Market and Yorkdale. It has also built a sixth-generation Waymo Driver autonomous driving system to navigate diverse environments, including the extreme winter weather Toronto faces in the colder months. A Waymo representative did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.
The company is also partnering with Toronto-based Element Fleet Management for vehicle maintenance, validation driving and customer service.

Waymo launched its fully autonomous ride service featuring electric vehicles in 2018. The ride service is currently available in the US in places including Miami, Phoenix and the San Francisco Bay Area. Earlier this year, Denver, San Diego, Las Vegas and Tampa were added to the list of available cities.
Sign-ups to ride with Waymo in Toronto and track the progress of the Canadian launch are now open on Waymo’s website.

articles.headline: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia fired after five days on the job
keyFacts: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her position after five days on the job, Al Jazeera confirmed.
Zacharia admitted to Fox News that she did not pass the bar exam after Trump described her as an attorney.
President Trump said there was no rush to hire Zacharia's replacement, according to Fox News.
body: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is “transitioning out” of her role just one week after United States President Donald Trump tapped her for the job, Al Jazeera has confirmed.
Fox News on Friday reported that Trump said there was no rush to hire Zacharia’s replacement.
Earlier Friday, Trump told reporters he told Zacharia to “reconsider” staying in the job.

“I don’t think Katie should be made to suffer like she’s suffering at the hands of the press,” Trump said as he departed the White House. “I said to her, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider. You think about it.’”
Zacharia said she had received a call about the role last week. She succeeded Karoline Leavitt.

Trump later announced her appointment and described her as an attorney. However, over the last week the question of whether Zacharia, a graduate of California’s Pepperdine University law school, had actually passed the bar exam to work as an attorney came under fire.
In an interview, she told Fox News on Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam.
She lasted five days on the job, half the length of Anthony Scaramucci’s tenure as director of communications, who served for 10 days during Trump’s first administration.
Al Jazeera correspondent Kimberly Halkett explained that the appointment and subsequent reversal could create further problems for Trump as Republicans prepare for a pivotal midterm election.

“The fact that there was that major credibility issue as well as a shaky performance is what sealed her fate,” said Halkett. “This makes the president look impulsive at a time when he’s already being criticised for not having a campaign that is really on track to win in November.”

articles.headline: Every DC Studios Movie and TV Show in Coming Through 2028 (and Beyond)
keyFacts: DC Studios co-chairmen and CEOs James Gunn and Peter Safran outlined upcoming DCU film and television projects spanning from 2026 through 2028 and beyond.
Upcoming theatrical releases include the body horror movie Clayface in October 2026, the Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow in July 2027, and The Batman Part 2 in February 2028.
Other announced projects include the mockumentary-style series The People v. Gorilla Grodd, an animated Dynamic Duo movie, and several undated films and series.
body: Since taking over the DC cinematic universe in 2022, DC Studios co-chairmen and CEOs James Gunn and Peter Safran have overhauled Warner Bros.' comic book-to-screen strategy. The new DCU officially launched in 2024 with the animated series Creature Commandos, and Gunn and Safran have since built out an all-new universe for the likes of Superman, Green Lantern, and Batman to play in. There have been ups and downs so far, as well as big shifts in Gunn's original vision for the DCU, which imagined a 10-year plan to explore the DC Universe across films, television, and video games.

There are still some lingering projects left over from the pre-Gunn era of the DCU, including a new Matt Reeves-led Batman movie and the fate of Peacemaker, the series starring John Cena that spanned two eras of DC film and television — and left fans contending with a major cliffhanger.
So, what's next for the DCU? Here’s everything DC is currently planning to put in theaters and on TV screens, this year and well into the future.
2026 DC Studios releases
Clayface
Release date: Oct. 23, in movie theaters

Clayface, a solo outing for the venerable Batman villain, wasn’t originally in James Gunn and Peter Safran’s plans for the DCU. But writer and filmmaker Mike Flanagan (Midnight Mass, Doctor Sleep) nonetheless impressed the DCU heads with his “horror-thriller-tragedy” idea, and now we’re getting a Clayface movie!

The body horror movie will offer a new take on Clayface’s origin story, with Tom Rhys Harries (White Lines, Suspicion) starring as Matt Hagen, a rising movie star who is brutally disfigured and turns to an experimental treatment to restore his good looks — with horrifying results.
Clayface is directed by James Watkins and also stars Naomi Ackie and Max Minghella.
2027 DC Studios releases
Man of Tomorrow
Release date: July 9, in movie theaters

Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow will be a story about Lex Luthor and Superman having to work together against a much, much bigger threat, according to Gunn. That big threat appears to be the alien Brainiac, who will be played by Lars Eidinger in the film.

Man of Tomorrow will see David Corenswet return as Clark Kent/Superman and Nicholas Hoult return as Lex Luthor. Also returning are Rachel Brosnahan as Lois Lane, Skyler Gisondo as Jimmy Olsen, Isabela Merced as Hawkgirl, Frank Grillo as Rick Flag Sr., María Gabriela de Faría as the Engineer, Sara Sampaio as Eve Teschmacher, and Milly Alcock as Supergirl. New to the cinematic Superman family are Aaron Pierre as John Stewart/Green Lantern and Adria Arjona, reportedly as the alien Maxima. Andre Royo, Matthew Lillard, and Sinqua Walls have been cast in unspecified roles.
The People v. Gorilla Grodd
Release date: TBD

The People v. Gorilla Grodd is a mockumentary-style series that will follow the Daily Planet's Jimmy Olsen investigating a murder case that centers on a psychic gorilla accused of patricide. HBO announced Friday has given the series an eight-episode, straight-to-series order for the new half-hour comedy that will draw comparisons to shows like The Office, Parks and Recreation, and American Vandal.

Superman's Skyler Gisondo will reprise his role as Jimmy Olsen and will costar alongside Jimmy Tatro as Gorilla Grodd. A handful of Superman actors will also return to the DCU for the series: Beck Bennett as Steve Lombard, Mikaela Hoover as Cat Grant, and Wendell Pierce as Perry White. The series also stars Mary Holland, Eduardo Franco, Arian Moayed, Dan Perrault, Andrew Leeds, and Tim Baltz. Tony Yacenda and Dan Perrault, who created American Vandal for Netflix, will serve as showrunners, writers, and executive producers.
2028 DC Studios releases
The Batman Part 2
Release date: Feb. 18, in movie theaters

The long, contentious history behind 2022’s The Batman didn’t leave much room for hope: As one of those movies that got bounced from team to team for years, changing shape at every bounce, it looked like a project destined to be driven more by market calculation than by a specific vision. But director and co-writer Matt Reeves found an effective take on The Dark Knight that resonated with audiences and landed solidly at the box office, and DC immediately greenlit a sequel, again with Robert Pattinson as the Caped Crusader.
The sequel has been a long time coming. Originally slated for a 2025 release, The Batman Part 2 has been delayed multiple times and is now an early 2028 release.

The Batman Part 2 will star Pattinson as Bruce Wayne/Batman, with Jeffrey Wright as Jim Gordon, Andy Serkis as Alfred Pennyworth, and Colin Farrell as Oz Cobb/The Penguin. They'll be joined by Sebastian Stan, Scarlett Johansson, and Charles Dance.
Dynamic Duo
Release date: June 30

Dynamic Duo is an animated movie about the origins of original Robin Dick Grayson and the second kid to fill his little green shoes, Jason Todd, a joint project between Gunn and Safran’s DC Studios and Warner Bros. Pictures Animation written by Matthew Aldrich (Coco, Lightyear).
Undated DC Studios projects
The Brave and the Bold

Taking its title from a Silver Age DC Comic that traditionally featured team-up stories, The Brave and the Bold will introduce Batman’s biological son Damian to the DCU — he’s the fifth of Batman’s many Robins — with a story inspired by Grant Morrison’s interpretation of the character in the Batman and Son run of the Batman comic. This will be Damian’s first appearance in a live-action film, though the character has appeared in animated form in TV and movies. The continuity of this film will be separate from Matt Reeves’ planned The Batman movies; it’s meant to establish the new DCU continuity for Batman and Robin.
Booster Gold

DC hasn’t said much about this TV series — except for Gunn announcing it as part of his and Safran’s new slate. It’s meant to bring the comics’ fan-favorite comic-relief character to the screen for his own comedic adventures. Show writer David Jenkins (Our Flag Means Death) was attached to the series, but he said that his take on the time-traveling superhero won't be moving forward. That doesn't mean that Booster Gold is dead, however.
Swamp Thing

Swamp Thing, a plant-elemental hero who (depending on which comics you’re reading) might or might not be a mutated version of scientist Alec Holland, dates back to 1971, and was successfully rebooted by Watchmen author Alan Moore in 1984. But it’ll be a while before we get to see what that looks like on the DC side.
Though Gunn has called Swamp Thing a “passion project” for James Mangold, the writer-director has a Star Wars movie to finish first — in theory.
Mister Miracle

Tom King and Mitch Gerads’ excellent 2017 limited series Mister Miracle is being adapted for animation. The animated series will tell the story of Scott Free, “the greatest escape artist who ever lived” as he tries to pull off the ultimate trick: escaping death itself. Mister Miracle, which is undated, will begin with something “[going] horribly wrong with the perfect life that Scott and his warrior wife Big Barda have built for themselves on Earth.”

In October 2026, DC Studios co-CEO Peter Safran confirmed some of the show's cast, which includes Josh Hutcherson (The Hunger Games) as Mister Miracle and Mackenzie Davis (Station Eleven) as his wife, Big Barda. Tom King, who recently served as co-creator of Lanterns, wrote all eight episodes of Mister Miracle himself, and Safran called the script "dynamite."
Blue Beetle animated series

Deadline reported in 2024 that Warner Bros. is developing an animated Blue Beetle series, focusing on the Jaime Reyes version of the character, as featured in 2023’s Blue Beetle. Miguel Puga, co-creator of the Nickelodeon series The Casagrandes, will serve as showrunner.
Untitled Wonder Woman movie

Rounding out DC Comics’ Big Three in the DCU is a planned new movie based on Wonder Woman. James Gunn confirmed to EW in June 2025 that the movie’s script is “being written right now.” And that’s about all that we know about it. But like Superman and various Batman projects, don’t expect any carryover from the Gal Gadot-led Wonder Woman movies.
Untitled Teen Titans movie

A live-action Teen Titans movie exists in very early form at DC Studios, with Supergirl screenwriter Ana Nogueira having turned in a draft of the in-development project, according to James Gunn. “It was something that Ana was really impassioned about, and she turned over an amazing script for us,” Gunn said in February. “She’s fiddling with that now, but it’s definitely not a finished script.”

The Teen Titans made their first appearance in 1964, with Kid Flash/Wally West, Robin/Dick Grayson, and Aqualad/Garth teaming up in The Brave and the Bold, later adding Wonder Girl/Donna Troy and many others (e.g., Cyborg, Beast Boy, Starfire, Raven) to their ranks. Of course, the Teen Titans already have an incredibly popular adaptation in the form of Teen Titans Go!, an animated Cartoon Network comedy series.
Savage Hunters

Batman and Robin/Nightwing nemeses Bane and Deathstroke are teaming up for a live-action movie of their own titled Savage Hunters. Peter Safran confirmed to reporters in February that screenwriter Matthew Orton (Moon Knight, Cleaner) is working on a script for DC Studios, which Gunn described as “something kind of like” a Deathstroke and Bane story.
What does this all mean? Maybe nothing, considering the long list of projects on DC Studios’ plate, but clearly the executives and creatives are trying anything and everyone for the new DCU.

articles.headline: You Can Play WoW: Forever For Free Next Week (But There’s A Catch)
keyFacts: Blizzard announced a free World of Warcraft: Forever beta stress test beginning October 19 requiring no subscription or paid beta access.
Blizzard stated the stress test will last only for a few hours to test servers, and all characters created during it will be deleted.
World of Warcraft: Forever is scheduled to launch on November 4, following early name reservations on October 27.
body: World of Warcraft: Forever's beta will be free for a limited time next week, giving players who want to check out the new version of Blizzard's old-school MMORPG but don't want to pay $60 for beta access a chance to see what all the hype is about.

Blizzard announced a WoW: Forever stress test will begin October 19 at 2 PM PT/ 5 PM ET, with no WoW subscription or beta access needed to play. The goal is to put the game's servers through their paces ahead of launch.
"This is a highly valuable event, since you'll participate in our discovering of issues that would have otherwise happened on launch day," Blizzard said in a post announcing the stress test.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dvueCoFTkCk&t

To install the test, players will need the Battle.net launcher installed and an account. After selecting WoW: Forever from the list of games, players can select to install the stress test under the "Game Version" drop-down menu.

There is, however, a catch. The stress test will only run for a "few hours," according to Blizzard. Exactly how long the test will last is still unclear. Blizzard said the test window "may end earlier or run later as needed." During the time that the stress test is live, the game's closed beta will be offline, but will return following the conclusion of the test. All characters made during the stress test will be deleted once the test is over.

It's not much, but for those who wanted to at least dabble in WoW: Forever without having to buy the $60 Skyborne Epic Pack for a beta code, the stress test will at least let curious players dip their toes in.

Even the beta itself won't be around for much longer. It will run until October 21, after which it will shut down and characters will be deleted to make way for early name reservations for the full game on October 27. WoW: Forever launches the following week on November 4.

All indicators so far point towards WoW: Forever's beta being a massive success . Multiple Blizzard developers have commented on how the game's popularity has already broken records, signaling launch could be huge.

The beta hasn't been all sunshine and rainbows, however. Multiple controversies have riled up the WoW community over the course of the beta, revealing WoW: Forever has a streamer problem . Illicit gold-buying scandals in the beta have pushed Blizzard to crack down on the practice harder than ever before (going so far as to add new in-game restrictions and warnings). Meanwhile, one controversial streamer is looking to create the biggest WoW guild ever seen and dominate the game's sole PvP server, much to the annoyance of regular players.
In a recent interview with GameSpot, Blizzard shared more details about WoW: Forever's future , and how it's trying to "push the envelope" on what players expect.

articles.headline: Dubois and Wardley at career-heaviest for rematch
keyFacts: Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley weighed in at their career-heaviest ahead of their heavyweight world-title rematch in London.
Dubois weighed 18st 2lb and Wardley weighed 17st 10lb before their Saturday meeting at the O2 Arena.
Promoter Frank Warren confirmed there is no clause for a third fight, but did not rule out a trilogy if Wardley wins.
body: - Published
Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley both weighed in at their career-heaviest and promised another explosive encounter in Saturday's heavyweight world-title rematch in London.
WBO champion Dubois tipped the scales at 18st 2lb (115kg) while Wardley came in at 17st 10lb (112kg) before their meeting at the O2 Arena.

The British rivals produced a fight-of-the-year contender in Manchester in May, with Wardley flooring Dubois twice before the Londoner rallied to stop his bloodied and battered opponent in the 11th round.
"I draw confidence from the successes I had in the first fight - getting knockdowns in the first and third," Wardley, 31, said.
"I need to capitalise on those moments better. I'm ready to put on a cleaner performance."
Dubois, 29, is more than 2lb heavier for the rematch, while Wardley has added more than 6lb.
Asked for his prediction, Wardley added: "Revenge, Fabio Wardley, knockout win."
Subdued scenes at Spitalfields Market
The final pre-fight formalities took place at Old Spitalfields Market in east London, with the two heavyweights taking to the scales amid the bustle of street-food stalls and shoppers.
A couple of hundred fans gathered beneath the market's Victorian roof, some having made the trip specifically for the event while others stopped to see what the fuss was about.
It was a rather subdued affair, with a smaller turnout than when Moses Itauma and Filip Hrgovic weighed in at the same venue in August.
Wardley arrived more than an hour before the event, appearing as relaxed as he has throughout fight week and even stopping for selfies with supporters afterwards.
Dubois arrived much later and has appeared in little mood for conversation this week. Once again, he was typically economical with his words.
"I know him now and know what to expect. I'm ready to go and do my job," the Londoner said. "I'm ready for a tear up. Let's go."
There was no drama at the obligatory face-off, despite the fierce rivalry that has developed between them, and two-time world champion Dubois was quick to leave the stage afterwards.
Could we see a trilogy?
With 41 knockouts between them from 43 victories, few expect the contest to go the distance.
Wardley, sporting Ipswich Town's newly-launched third kit with his name printed on the sleeve, was still bearing the scars of his punishing defeat in Manchester five months ago.
A cut across the bridge of his nose, first sustained during his 2024 draw with Frazer Clarke, reopened against Dubois and left his face badly swollen and bloodied.
The punishment he absorbed has raised questions over whether his decision to take an immediate rematch has come too soon but Wardley remains confident he can reverse the result.
"It's simply seek and destroy now," he said.
Promoter Frank Warren is predicting a "blockbuster" 2027 for the heavyweight division, with lucrative fights awaiting Saturday's winner.
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will finally meet in Cardiff on 11 December, while British prospect Itauma is set to return in January following his world-title defeat by Hrgovic.

Warren confirmed there is no clause for a third fight between Dubois and Wardley but the Queensberry Promotions boss refused to rule out a trilogy if the Ipswich fighter avenges the only defeat on his record.
"If that happens it's a natural fight," Warren said. "That's what's so intriguing about this. Who will they fight next year? We want to find out who is the best."

articles.headline: Why Apple is finally making its own smart home devices
keyFacts: Apple launched the Apple Home Collection smart home lineup and HomeView smart display, codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.
Apple ranks third in smart home platform adoption behind Amazon and Google, according to research from Parks Associates.
Apple is partnering with ADT through its retail stores to help customers install the new devices.
body: For more than a decade, Apple has told other companies to build smart home devices for its platform. This week, Apple launched its own. The Apple Home Collection is a lineup of cameras, thermostats, sensors, a smart door lock, and a video doorbell, all codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. They arrive alongside HomeView, Apple’s first smart display.
Why Apple is finally making its own smart home devices

Apple’s new smart home lineup promises easier setup, tighter integration, and data privacy. But with steep competition and steeper prices, can Apple convince more people to adopt its vision of the smart home?
Why Apple is finally making its own smart home devices

Apple’s new smart home lineup promises easier setup, tighter integration, and data privacy. But with steep competition and steeper prices, can Apple convince more people to adopt its vision of the smart home?

Even after 12 years of HomeKit, Apple’s smart home ecosystem still feels underdeveloped, especially compared to the competition. Amazon’s and Google’s ecosystems support more products, and both have popular in-house brands: Ring and Nest. Apple had nothing of its own to point customers to as an Apple experience — and now it does.

But why now? And does Apple actually add anything new here, or is this mostly packaging? At Apple’s “Welcome home” event in New York this week, I spoke with Kaiann Drance, vice president of product marketing for home at Apple, about the company’s new approach to the smart home and what this means for Apple’s commitment to Matter, the interoperable open smart home standard it helped found.
Why now?

Drance says the big reason was the development of the right technologies. The first was Matter, which provided the ecosystem. The second was AI, which brought a more conversational Siri voice assistant. Both were necessary to create a dedicated home device in HomeView. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” Drance says. “That’s been a really critical piece of bringing this all together.”
The bigger play is HomeView as a gateway to the smart home.

The bigger play here is HomeView as a gateway to the smart home for Apple’s users. Buy one for playing music, guided cooking recipes, and checking your calendar, and you might soon want a camera or smart lock to go with it. Drance says they’ve seen that once people try a single smart device and find it easier than they expected, it “unlocks this delightful understanding of what’s possible once you bring these products into the home.” She argues that most people just don’t know what a smart home can do.

She’s not wrong. The biggest barrier to buying smart devices is that people don’t see any value in the products, according to research from Parks Associates. Privacy and security concerns and complexity also rank high, along with cost. While Apple isn’t addressing the cost concern here — the products start at $200 — the other elements are part of its pitch: one-tap setup, your data stays yours, one app to run it all. Apple’s stamp of approval also carries a lot of weight. “People who own Apple products are very, very loyal, and there is a large user base,” says Elizabeth Parks, president and CMO at Parks Associates.
From a choose-your-own adventure to a tailored solution

Until now, Apple Home has been a bit like a buffet: You can pick from any brand that supports HomeKit or Matter and hope it all goes together. The Home Collection is more like the chef’s choice, a short list of dishes Apple promises will pair well. Drance says that’s what some customers were asking for. “There is a lot of choice with Matter, and there’s a lot of great products out there,” she says. “But sometimes we do get asked, ‘Hey, what product should I put in the home?’”

Rather than build devices itself, Apple chose to codevelop the lineup with partners that “have their own expertise in the home.” Both have a global footprint and home experience, she says, “LG more so in consumer products, Schneider through home build and home installations.” Drance says it was a ground-up collaboration with Apple bringing “the design aesthetic that would be suitable for the home and suitable to go with our family of products.” The company is also partnering with ADT through Apple retail stores to help people install the devices.

Drance says setup and ease of use were a big focus. “The one-tap setup was really important to make it so easy, having no need for a separate account, no need for a separate app,” she says. “We just wanted that simplicity to be at its core, and of course, the privacy that we’ve developed together with our partners.” She says everything integrates through Apple Home; you don’t need to create an LG or Schneider account, and all data is end-to-end encrypted, so only you can access it.

Drance was clear that the Apple Home Collection isn’t replacing the buffet — the hardware ecosystem that has grown up around Apple Home. “We still have this incredible ecosystem with Matter, and with Works with Apple Home, that is going to remain,” she says. “We know that homes are not a one-size-fits-all solution, so our customers will continue to have that choice, and we remain committed to building that ecosystem as well.”

The hardware mostly backs that up. The lock, thermostats, and sensors are Matter-compatible; the lock supports Aliro and works entirely locally, and every device supports Thread. The exception is the cameras, which use Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video, not Matter. That’s the biggest lock-in. I was surprised Apple didn’t announce Matter camera support. But the Thread radios suggest the hardware might be Matter-ready, and Apple may be waiting for the Matter camera standard to support encrypted uploads, something HKSV already does.
So, what’s the benefit?

Does the Home Collection do anything other Apple Home devices can’t? In theory, no; in practice, yes. “What we’ve done with Apple Home Collection is we’ve added another layer on top of that, that deeper integration,” says Drance. There aren’t features exclusive to the Home Collection; it’s more that Apple is saying all the features will be here. It’s a bit like Google making a Pixel phone to show Android developers what Android can do: Apple’s products come with the full suite of capabilities the platform offers.
“The one-tap setup was really important to make it so easy, having no need for a separate account, no need for a separate app.”
— Kaiann Drance, Apple

According to Apple, setup is as simple as tapping your iPhone to the device, like pairing AirPods, with no extra account or app needed and no scanning required. Every device uses Thread to stay connected if Wi-Fi drops, and Apple says each can update its own network credentials when you change your Wi-Fi. This could address the offline-device problems that plague Apple Home. Everything is end-to-end encrypted, and the cameras keep recording to onboard storage if your Wi-Fi drops.

The devices also support Apple Home features other manufacturers have been slow to adopt. The LG lock is only the third to offer hands-free Home Key unlocking over UWB, and both thermostats work with Apple’s Clean Energy Guidance and Adaptive Temperature, which adjusts around your location and sleep schedule.
At least that’s the promise. We’ll have to test these devices to see how well they deliver.
A curated garden path

Together, Apple’s new devices form a polished, cohesive starter kit for the smart home — albeit an expensive one. The cameras, lock, and thermostats cost $200 to $400, and camera history requires an iCloud Plus plan. As Drance said, the smart home isn’t a one-size-fits-all solution, so this won’t work for everybody. If you already have a Ring doorbell or Google Nest Hub, this probably isn’t for you. Instead, Apple is trying to guide its existing customers who haven’t bought a video doorbell or smart lock yet down a curated path into the smart home.

However, Apple faces a tougher challenge in the broader market: It’s arriving late. The smart display category is already mature; millions of homes have Echo and Google smart displays. Millions more have Ring or Nest doorbells, neither of which will work with HomeView at launch.

As a smart home platform, Apple Home ranks third in adoption, behind Google, with Amazon holding a big lead, according to Parks Associates research. But customer loyalty to those platforms isn’t guaranteed. Four in five smart-home households would consider switching, Parks says, especially if another platform lets them control everything in one place. “Interoperability will be critical, but the bigger prize is owning the consumer relationship,” she says.
With its Home Collection, Apple isn’t reinventing the smart home; it’s trying to make it easier to get into one.

articles.headline: Katie Zacharia fired after five days as White House press secretary
keyFacts: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was fired on Friday, just five days after assuming the role, a White House official said.
Zacharia faced scrutiny following her first press briefing and questions regarding her credentials after confirming she failed the bar exam.
Donald Trump told reporters he asked Zacharia to reconsider her role following increasing scrutiny and negative media attention.
body: Donald Trump’s new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, was fired on Friday, just five days after she assumed the role, according to a White House official.

The person was not authorized to speak publicly about the decision, which had not been formally announced. Zacharia had a rocky start to her tenure as press secretary, hosting a widely panned first White House press briefing on Tuesday. She had also faced questions over her legal credentials after admitting she did not pass the bar exam.
Zacharia, a little-known conservative political commentator who spent much of her career in communication roles, was offered the White House press secretary role on 9 October.
In an interview with the Guardian on Thursday, she detailed the whirlwind sprint to the podium to replace Karoline Leavitt as the president’s chief spokesperson.
But on Friday, Trumptold reporters he had asked Zacharia to “reconsider” serving as press secretary, after increasing scrutiny and negative media attention.

“I said, ‘Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don’t need it,’” Trump said, speaking with reporters outside the White House. “I said to her, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider. You think about it, but I would reconsider.’”

During her first press briefing, Zacharia stumbled through prepared remarks highlighting Trump’s accomplishments in his presidency. She made a notable gaffe when she called her husband “the president”.
Members of the White House press corps were left puzzled when she ended the briefing after only taking questions from three predominantly conservative media outlets.

Questions about Zacharia’s resume grew in the following days after reports emerged revealing Zacharia, who described herself as a lawyer, never passed the bar exam. She later confirmed she took the bar once and failed.

Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University’s law school and shared social media posts that identified herself as an “attorney”. Trump had also called Zacharia an “attorney” when announcing her appointment.
She defended describing herself as a “lawyer”, claiming there was a difference between a “lawyer” and an “attorney”.

Over the last few days, Zacharia spoke with members of the media, in an effort to try to clarify her legal credentials and make the case that she was ready to take on the role as the president’s chief spokesperson.
In an unexpectedly tough interview on Thursday evening, Fox host Sean Hannity grilled Zacharia about her first press briefing, asking bluntly: “What happened?”

Zacharia sought to explain that she had little time to prep in the days between accepting the job and holding her first press briefing and argued that the conservative Daily Mail, one of only three outlets she took questions from, was “not known to be a conservative outlet”. Hannity, a Trump ally, also pressed her on her decision to identify herself as a “lawyer”.
“Why get into this long-drawn-out definition of the difference between a lawyer and an attorney? Because I don’t think most people see much of a distinction,” he asked.

On Friday morning, Lawrence Jones, a Fox & Friends host, continued, telling Zacharia: “You know, Katie, it’s been a tough week for you. It’s not an easy job to be the press secretary, and you never want to be the story.”
Speaking to reporters, Trump said the interviewers had been “a little tough” on Zacharia.
“She’s been treated, I would say, pretty nastily,” the president said.

articles.headline: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
keyFacts: The Australian government introduced legislation requiring social media platforms to allow users to turn off algorithmically recommended content.
Officials said the proposed bill aims to protect users from online harms, imposing potential fines of up to A$100 million for non-compliance.
Critics and the Trump administration argued the reforms threaten free speech, while major tech companies largely declined to comment.
body: - Published
Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder
Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.

Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.
Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.
"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.
"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."
Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.
It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.

The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.
It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.

Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws â which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services â will help Australians become happier and healthier.

But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.
The choice
Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.
Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.
It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.
He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order.
"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC.

"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."
The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.
Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."
Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.

Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see â and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.
Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.
But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.

Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction, external; that algorithms â often unsolicited â serve up content which harms users' mental health, external, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline.
Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line.

"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.
While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change.
"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.

Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s â a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.
More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.

The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off.
"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said.
"If people want to doom scrollâ¦ that's fine, that's up to them."

The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services â social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more â to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".

Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features â for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women â and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (Â£52m, $70m).

"The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC.
The challenges

There's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation.

In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive â although a US jury recently ruled otherwise.
"I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' â like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' â and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney.
Right-wing parties in Australia â and the Trump administration â have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship.

But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake â they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week.
The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children.

However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued.
The EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 â after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds â is a cautionary tale.

Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that.

"Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation, external.

On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return.
The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act.

The rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app.
Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global.
"We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing."
Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them.

Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment."
Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms â though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off.
Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice.
"On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good."

If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line.

articles.headline: Oil surges to $110 per barrel for the first time since May
keyFacts: Brent crude oil surpassed $110 per barrel on Friday, reaching its highest level since May as wars threatened global energy supplies.
President Donald Trump eased sanctions on Russia to reduce diesel costs, drawing condemnation from lawmakers in both political parties.
Friday's energy price increases will likely raise gasoline costs for United States consumers in the coming days.
body: A key oil price benchmark surged Friday to its highest level in five months, as investors assessed the impact of both the Iran and Ukraine-Russia wars on global energy supplies.
Brent crude oil, widely considered to be among the most important prices in global energy, surpassed $110 per barrel shortly after 2:30 p.m. ET, its highest level since May.

U.S. crude oil, which also steers gas prices, jumped 3.5% Friday to close at $101.41 per barrel. It was the first time West Texas Intermediate crude had crossed the $100 threshold, closely watched by both traders and the public, since September.
Friday’s price jumps will likely add to already elevated gasoline prices for U.S. consumers in coming days. As of Friday morning, regular gasoline averaged $4.32 per gallon nationwide.
Diesel futures also jumped by more than 1% Friday. The cost of this commercial fuel critical for farming and other industrial sectors has risen even faster than regular gasoline in recent months.
Stocks fell Friday, partly in response to the jump in energy prices. The S&P 500 fell more than 1% while the Nasdaq Composite sharply dropped 2% by midafternoon.
The price of fuel around the world began its steady rise this spring, when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February, prompting the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
But an escalation in the Russia-Ukraine war in recent months has caused an even more dramatic price spike for diesel.

Russia has traditionally been one of the world’s largest diesel exporters. But attack by Ukrainian forces on its energy infrastructure has taken much of its refining capacity offline. Likewise, energy assets in Ukraine have been targeted by Russian strikes.
As a result of the strikes, buyers of Russian diesel have been forced to look elsewhere for their fuel supplies.

But there aren’t any clear opportunities to easily expand diesel production. Refineries in the U.S. and Europe are already running at nearly maximum capacity to churn out as much diesel fuel as possible.
President Donald Trump is intensely focused on the high cost of diesel fuel because of its key role in driving up inflation -- a top issue for American voters in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Trump has pressured U.S. allies to release some of their diesel and crude oil reserves, and he recently signed an order to ease regulations on the use of off-road “red dye” diesel.
When neither of these actions resulted in a significant step down for diesel prices, Trump made the decision this month to ease U.S. sanctions on Russia.
The goal was to allow Russian President Vladimir Putin to release some of Russia’s supplies to the global market.
But the sanctions relief stunned world leaders and drew quick condemnation from U.S. lawmakers in both parties.
While Trump has touted the deal with Putin as a way to lower prices, as of Friday, no actual Russian diesel had been identified as having reached the global market.

Russia’s refining infrastructure has been badly damaged by Ukrainian strikes. On Friday, another Russian refiner suspended some crude oil operations. The Russian Defense Ministry said Ukraine had “attempted a massive attack on the Ryazan oil refinery.”
Additionally, a group of American lawmakers introduced a bill that would block Trump’s deal for Russian diesel. It has little chance of passing the Republican-controlled House.

But polling indicates that Republicans are unlikely to maintain a majority in the House after November’s elections. The Russian diesel blocking bill offers a preview of the kind of legislation that could advance under Democratic control.
Yet even now, the legislation adds to “growing doubts that a U.S. — Russia diesel deal will come to fruition,” said Mason Mendez, global real assets analyst at Wells Fargo.
“Investors also remain concerned about further military escalation in the Middle East, as attacks on commercial shipping and regional infrastructure have increased in recent weeks,” he said.
“Looking into 2027, the need to rebuild depleted global inventories could create an additional source of demand and keep energy prices elevated for longer.”

articles.headline: Nonolith traps you in a living maze and challenges you to find hidden terrain magic using good old copy-paste
keyFacts: Nonolith is a 2D puzzle game created by Justcamh where players control a gnome trapped inside a living edifice.
Players can copy, paste, move, rotate, and delete chunks of scenery or activate hidden spells using tile patterns to escape.
A demo is currently available on Steam, and the full game is scheduled for release later this year.
body: After enjoying Echo Weaver last week, I'm in the market for games that gaze with utmost scorn upon the concept of unlockable abilities, smugly declaring that everything you need to complete them is available to you from the word go.

There was a time when the idea of a game without unlocks wasn't all that novel, you know. Indeed, you young people may be surprised to hear that videogames pre-date the act of unlocking. Genesis-era Sonic the Hedgehog never unlocked so much as a +5% SPD perk. Still, Genesis-era Sonic wasn't a bizarrely malleable 2D puzzler like Nonolith. Created by Justcamh, it casts you as a hapless gnome who is trapped inside a colossal living edifice. Aside from running and jumping, you have the power to copy-paste, move, rotate or delete chunks of the very scenery.

At its simplest, this might involve lifting a wall out of the way, or cropping pieces of hanging stone to create a staircase. But there are also hidden spells you can activate by arranging the tiles into certain patterns, in addition to more familiar props such as pistons that shove other blocks around.

There are nine "worlds" within the Nonolith, arranged on a 3X3 grid, and they can be completed many ways. The overall goal is to escape, but if all you do is escape, the Steam page will be deeply disappointed in you. "For the most adventurous, escape is only the beginning," it thrills. "Reach the highest level of mastery and the Nonolith will succumb to your will. Power awaits the few who dare to wield ultimate control."
There's a Nonolith demo on Steam, with the full game coming later this year. I get a slight Animal Well and/or Fez vibe from the thing, though both of those trade in dastardly unlockables.

articles.headline: Game, set and tache: Carlos Alcaraz joins growing trend for a stylish top lip
keyFacts: Tennis player Carlos Alcaraz debuted a new moustache at the Shanghai Masters after he and his team agreed to grow them if he won the Japan Open.
Barbers and cultural scholars report that thin moustaches are making a significant comeback among young men and male celebrities.
Scholars suggest the trend allows young men to signal maturity, curate a specific form of manliness, and distance themselves from heavy beards.
body: The tennis superstar Carlos Alcaraz might have been knocked out of the Shanghai Masters in straight sets earlier this week, but he did so sporting a moustache that became almost as remarked upon as his aptitude for a sneaky drop shot.

“I always wanted to step on the court at least once with the moustache,” Alcaraz said. The Spaniard and his team had all agreed to take the facial-hair plunge if he won the Japan Open, which he did for a second straight year. “¡Bigotes para todos!” or “moustaches for everyone”, they apparently cheered at the end of the match.
At Milan fashion week last month, the Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi sported a thin strip of hair on his top lip as he watched his girlfriend, Kendall Jenner, model for the Bottega Veneta show.

A moustachioed Harry Styles is roughly halfway through his record-breaking 30-show residency at Madison Square Garden in New York. The actor Timothée Chalamet, who kept his Marty Supreme ’tache on throughout awards season, has been playing around with his facial hair again, adding a goatee.
On TikTok, gen Z men with moustaches are plentiful, as are tutorials for how to grow and style them – alongside almost as many videos from older generations questioning them.

High street barber shops are seeing evidence of it, too. At Citadel in Sheffield, more young men are asking for moustaches, and a large number are asking specifically for thin ones, which the owner, Marie Williams, describes as “[a] low maintenance, easygoing moustache that’s attainable to most”.
According to Jay Byrne, a barber at Dog House barbers in Birmingham and a former British barber of the year: “The moustache is certainly making a comeback, particularly among younger men.”
The moustaches appearing on young men’s faces are a long way from the bushier ones seen in the 1970s and 80s, epitomised by Tom Selleck in Magnum PI.

They seem more to hark back to the Hollywood stars of the 40s and 50s such as David Niven and Clark Gable. “We’re seeing a move away from the heavier, traditional moustaches … towards a much more refined, deliberately styled look,” says Byrne.

“Achieving the look is all about precision, proportion and understanding what suits the individual’s facial structure. It’s not simply a case of growing a moustache and leaving it alone. The shape, thickness and detailing are what make the difference.”
According to Dr Ashley Morgan, a masculinities scholar at Cardiff Metropolitan University: “Skinny moustaches are a sign of difference, especially from men who keep beards.”

Given the rise of the manosphere and the complicated state of masculinity at the moment, Morgan thinks these skinnier moustaches could be intended to steer clear of signalling alpha masculinity. “Young men want to demonstrate a carefully curated form of ‘manliness’,” she says.
For these young male celebrities in particular, Morgan thinks it could be “an expression of ageing”.

“Timothée Chamalet is 30, Jacob Elordi is 29 … it could well be a sign that they want to show that they are mature, they have entered a new phase of life, and want to be seen as more ‘manly’ while remaining youthful.”

For 34-year-old Ncuti Gatwa, who starred in the most recent series of Doctor Who, it has certainly been a way to lean into his age after making his name while playing a schoolboy in the hit TV drama Sex Education.
Gatwa told the Radio Times: “I’d spent the last four years playing a child [in Sex Education], at the age of 30, so I said: ‘Let me have my moustache back.’”

The fashion historian Tony Glenville once had a curly moustache but, he says, “like many men, [I] got rid of facial hair during the mask-wearing times of Covid”. He says it is a trend “among young men who’ve not really seen it around so much recently”. Facial hair, as with all things, “has huge fashion phases for men”.

Movember, which launched in 2003 and has grown into a global movement, sees men grow moustaches for the month of November to raise money for charity and has arguably made facial hair more popular again.
For such a small slither of hair, the moustache is historically and culturally freighted. It can symbolise freedom and has long held a central position in gay culture.

While the moustache might be a “trend” in western culture, in other cultures it is much more of a constant. From romance to war, religion to masculinity and sexuality, moustaches connote different things in different contexts.
Luckily for anyone wanting to give a thin moustache a whirl, according to barber Williams, it is a style that “requires minimal upkeep; just a few snips with the scissors to maintain”.

articles.headline: RFK Jr. proposes FDA look the other way on unproven peptides, report says
keyFacts: The FDA submitted an interim access policy on unproven peptide drugs for White House review, according to a government filing notice.
People familiar with the proposal told The Associated Press that it would grant the FDA enforcement discretion on certain peptide drugs.
The proposal follows a 2023 FDA determination that the peptides lacked safety and efficacy data and posed potential risks.
body: Under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the Food and Drug Administration is moving forward with plans to ease access to unproven peptide drugs that are popular among members of Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement—despite FDA staff scientists finding that the drugs have not been sufficiently studied to establish safety and efficacy and may cause harms.

The FDA submitted an “Interim Access Policy” on peptides for review by the White House, according to a filing notice posted on an Office of Management and Budget website. The posting does not provide information on the proposed policy. But people familiar with the proposal told The Associated Press that it would give the FDA “enforcement discretion” on certain peptide drugs. This would allow the agency to choose not to enforce current restrictions on peptides and provide an assurance to specialty pharmacies eager to start making them that they will not be targeted by the agency.
The Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the FDA, did not respond to a request for comment from Ars Technica.

The proposal comes as the FDA is currently re-reviewing a dozen popular, but unproven, injectable peptide drugs. In 2023, FDA scientists determined that the peptides lacked data on safety and efficacy and posed risks. As such, they were stricken from a list of drugs that can be made by specialty pharmacies, called compounding pharmacies, which make customized formulas for drugs.
“Charlatans”

Still, the dodgy drugs have grown more popular, with sellers claiming, without evidence, that the drugs can improve appearance, boost energy, and help heal injuries, among other wellness claims. They’re especially popular among the MAHA crowd; many prominent MAHA figures sell peptide products, and Kennedy, a self-proclaimed “big fan” of peptides, vowed to end “FDA’s war” on peptides upon taking office.

articles.headline: Analogue returns to the 16-bit era with the Mega Sg+ and Super Nt+
keyFacts: Analogue announced the Super Nt+ and Mega Sg+, updated FPGA retro consoles that play original Super Nintendo and Sega Genesis cartridges on modern TVs.
The $220 systems add wireless controller support, USB-C power, hot-swappable cartridges, and a redesigned case, though controllers are sold separately.
Analogue stated that pre-orders begin on Monday, October 19, with shipping scheduled to start in December.
body: Analogue returns to the 16-bit era with the Mega Sg+ and Super Nt+
Dust off your old Sega Genesis and Super Nintendo cartridges.

Analogue is revisiting the console rivalry that defined the first half of the 1990s. On Friday, the company announced the Super Nt+ and Mega Sg+, updated versions of its Super Nintendo and Sega Genesis throwback consoles. Each costs $220, with shipping planned for December.

Like Analogue's Super Nt (2018) and Mega Sg (2019), these are FPGA systems, which recreate the original hardware on a chip rather than emulate games in software. The advantage is that you get lag-free 16-bit games on a modern TV — all without having to hunt down ROMs. But the flip side is you'll need to bring your own original cartridges. Think of it like the gaming equivalent of a modern record player for your old vinyl collection.
What's new

The big hardware upgrade is wireless controller support. Both consoles now have built-in Bluetooth and 2.4GHz. There's a dedicated pairing button for the gamepads of your choice, and you can power the systems on and off from the primary controller. Wired controllers are still supported. However, no gamepads are included with the consoles, so you'll want to factor that into the cost. 8BitDo's retro-style M30 and SN30 controllers, which match the respective Sega and Nintendo aesthetics, cost $30 apiece.

The consoles add USB-C power and a USB-A port, which you can use to connect CRTs or charge controllers. There's an SD card slot onboard. The systems also have a new OS and a redesigned case. And you can now swap cartridges without shutting down the system.
Analogue says each console plays 2,200+ games, region-free. The Mega Sg+ still has a Sega CD connector and comes with a Master System adapter. Video maxes out at 1080p, with no 4K support.

You can pre-order the Super Nt+ and Mega Sg+ from Analogue's website starting on Monday, October 19, at 8AM PT. Each costs $220, plus controller costs if you don't already have them. Shipping is expected to start in December.

articles.headline: Israeli settlers beat Palestinians and a U.S. photojournalist in West Bank attacks
keyFacts: Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians harvesting olives and injured several people, including an American photojournalist, in the West Bank.
Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine was beaten and hospitalized while reporting on the olive harvest, the newspaper said.
Israeli police stated they would investigate reports of the injured foreign journalist and bring those involved to justice.
body: Israeli settlers beat Palestinians and a U.S. photojournalist in West Bank attacks
Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians as they were harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank on Friday, injuring several people including an American photojournalist.
The Washington Post said photographer Heidi Levine was reporting in the West Bank, wearing a protective vest clearly marked as "press," when she was beaten.

"Today I was brutally attacked," Levine said in a video filmed at a hospital and posted online."We saw in the distance, in the hilltop, I would say at least 50 masked men, slingshots. And when they came running down, I was attacked, pushed to the ground," she said, "they just kept kicking me and kicking me." They also stole her cameras and phone.

She said medical workers rushed her in an ambulance to a hospital. Washington Post Executive Editor Matt Murray said in a statement the paper was relieved that Levine received medical care and is safe, but denounced the violence against her.
"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," Murray said.
The Post said the attack happened when Palestinians were trying to harvest their olives. It said settlers set Palestinian olive groves on fire and hurled stones using slingshots.
Israeli police issued a statement acknowledging reports that a foreign journalist was injured and said it would investigate the incident and "bring those involved to justice."

The U.S. State Department said it was aware of the reports and contacted The Washington Post to offer consular assistance. "We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and support appropriate investigations as well as legal accountability for those responsible," the State Department said, without mentioning the assault of the American photojournalist.
There were two dozen settler attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters Friday, leaving 20 people injured, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent Society.

The United Nations' humanitarian office for Gaza and the West Bank said settler attacks during the olive harvest season have killed one Palestinian and damaged more than 2,500 olive trees or saplings.

The attacks came as groups of Israeli settlers have stepped up their assaults on Palestinians in the West Bank. They also follow another assault earlier this month, when Israelis beat Agence France-Presse photojournalist Jaafar Ashtiyeh as he was covering settler violence against Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank.

Sara Qudah, who handles the Middle East for the Committee to Protect Journalists, said Levine's beating was not an isolated incident for journalists covering the West Bank olive harvest. "It's part of a disturbing pattern of violence and harassment against journalists regardless of their nationalities," she said.
She added that the attackers have no reason to fear consequences because Israeli authorities fail to do anything to stop the violence.
The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate also condemned the attack as an "assault on press freedom" and a violation of rules protecting journalists during conflicts.
Nuha Musleh contributed reporting from Ramallah, West Bank.

articles.headline: The case for data centers, explained by a person who wants you to like them
keyFacts: A recent Gallup poll found that 71 percent of Americans oppose building AI data centers in their communities.
Nicole Thomas, a public relations representative for data centers, stated that the industry is facing severe public backlash and must improve community education.
Thomas explained that public opposition to data centers is often driven by broader fears and concerns regarding artificial intelligence.
body: The JPMorgan Chase data center in Orangeburg, New York, on October 14, 2026. | Kena Betancur/Getty Images

Lately, AI data centers are public enemy No. 1. The concerns are legion: how much water and electricity they consume, the noise they generate, the sprawling buildings they bring to communities, and the technology they’re powering that may or may not take all of our jobs and usher in the robot apocalypse.

Earlier this year, Gallup found that 71 percent of Americans oppose building data centers that support AI in their communities. And the backlash is bipartisan: Majorities of Democrats, Republicans, and independents opposed local construction.

Even in Texas, where data center development has been booming, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott has hit the brakes . In September, he directed state regulators to halt permits for data centers pending audits examining their effects on the power grid and water resources.
But while many data center projects have run aground, others are still getting built — and the companies behind them are employing experts like Nicole Thomas to smooth the way.

Thomas is the senior vice president of media and community engagement at JSA, a marketing and public relations firm that represents data center companies. She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram about how the industry is responding to public opposition — and why she argues that these facilities can still be good neighbors.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .
You’ve been at this for 21 years. Obviously, 21 years ago, data centers were not the hot-button issue they are today. When did you notice the shift?

I’d say about two years ago. I came into this industry myself about four and a half years ago. I come from a state transportation background where community engagement is just paramount. When you’re putting a new traffic intersection up, they expect you to interact with the public.

When I got to this industry, I said, “Oh, what’s your community engagement like?” And they said, “We don’t even have any community engagements in this industry.” And they weren’t wrong. Because 21 years ago, [data centers] were just like infrastructure. It was like building a warehouse for your computers. And so it was very similar to the way that you would build a Costco.

You would just go in, request a zoning permit, the zoning board would say, “Yeah, that works. Stamp, boom.” And you build your data center. And as a matter of fact, it was very secretive before, because data, and having that data in the wrong hands, has a lot of [cybersecurity] implications. About two years ago is when we started noticing the mainstream journalists coming around asking questions about data centers. And that’s, to me, when it started.

It still feels secretive, I think, to a lot of people, and that’s why people are mad. If you read about this data center that was proposed in Utah by Mr. Wonderful, Kevin O’Leary , it caught a lot of people off guard. Seventy percent of Americans, at the moment, do not want them in their backyards. How do you go about trying to change that 70 percent’s minds?

First and foremost, I think education is really important. And so one of the things that we did notice very early on because of the previously secretive nature of data centers, there wasn’t a lot of education out there about what they even are. And so that’s something we need to change. We need to make the connection between [phones] and data centers so that people understand what a data center means to their life on a daily basis.

Every app on your cellphone requires a data center to save your information in there. When you put your password into anything, you are interacting with a data center, which will verify your password and then let you into that app. Not to mention all of the information about you that you store in that app is then stored in a data center so that it can be recalled at any time.

We could not be having this call without digital infrastructure. It doesn’t work that way. We can’t have email without digital infrastructure. And that stat about 70 percent of people not wanting the data center in their backyard — I’d be interested in seeing the stat of how many people actually live near a data center and don’t realize it.

Because there are nondescript data centers doing work quietly in your neighborhood that have been there for decades and you don’t even know it. And so in some ways I feel, and I think the industry does as a whole, but I won’t speak for them, that the pushback on data centers is somewhat related to the pushback on AI, because people can’t control AI.

You even have Sam Altman telling us that AI will destroy society. So you have this concern about AI and you don’t know how to control it, but you can push back on data centers. And so it becomes the physical manifestation of AI are these data centers that people are trying to get overturned or get to not be in their neighborhoods.

It’s understandable. I’m a citizen too. You’re a citizen, and if things come into my neighborhood, I want to know about them. I have questions. There’s a big data center that just came to my community not long ago and their community engagement was horrible, absolutely horrible.
Can I ask where you are?

I’m in Indiana and I won’t say which hyperscaler it is, but a hyperscaler came into — I would say, not my neighborhood, into my city. They’re definitely not in my backyard, but they’re in my city. And so we took them to task because their community engagement was basically non-existent.
Wait, you work in data center PR, but you took a data center in your community to task for not being transparent enough?
Yeah, absolutely.
Which side are you on?
I’m on the side of responsible development.
We’ve all kind of accepted that we need a cloud for X, Y, and Z. And that it’s worth it so I can take lots of photos. I think everyone’s cool with that.

But the issue here is that people aren’t necessarily cool with AI, but we’re barreling forward anyway. How do you separate this essential need we have from AI, which people don’t necessarily feel is essential to their lives?

I think it goes back to education. Educating consumers on the difference between data centers: a small data center, a medium data center, a large data center. Educating them on why data centers exist and how they interact with data centers on a daily basis multiple times.

I hear you. But again, I feel like the issue here is not the data centers my cellphone needs, but instead is the data centers these AI companies need and these AI companies who the public doesn’t necessarily trust because they keep telling us that they’re going to kill us, and who the public is wary of because they don’t want their jobs being replaced by AI.
There’s all sorts of reasons that people are skeptical of new technology. So how do you specifically respond to that fear and to those people?

I think it’s, again, understanding the actual data center that’s being built in your community. Is it a 5-megawatt data center? That’s never going to house AI. That’s not enough power to house AI. Is it a one-gigawatt data center like Mr. Wonderful in Utah? That’s different.

But I think that AI is probably going to be something that is a lightning rod in the American public for a very long time. There are going to be people who are going to be anti-AI and pro-AI, and there’s going to be some people in the middle. I think it’s just, again, for us, it’s education, educating the community.
Have you ever been part of a project that a community rejected and you guys just packed up and said, “Okay, we’ll go find another community? ”
Yeah. We have some clients who have had pushback from residents and they have said, “Let’s do a one-on-one community meeting where people can come in and ask us questions.”

And after the questions were answered, the community leaves and says, “Okay, this isn’t as bad as I thought it was.” Or we have a community that says, “No, we now have a moratorium and we’re pushing all data centers away.“

Sometimes they’ll wait for their client — my client is a developer and they’ve got clients that they’re developing for. If that client will wait, then maybe it is something that we’ll try to work out with the community. But oftentimes, they’ll just say, there’s communities who are literally raising their hand saying, “We’ll take a data center. We’ll take one. We’ll take two. Bring it here.”

So there are communities who recognize the benefits of data centers. And there are going to be other communities who say, “No, we don’t want this.” And then in five, six, eight years, they’re going to be like, “Wow, that county has a lot of tax dollars. They have a lot of really cool stuff. Why don’t we have that?” And the answer will be data centers.

I don’t think this ends anytime soon though, right? I counsel my clients that we could still be here in three to five years, really trying to help the American public understand the benefit of data centers. But it’s going to take a lot of education across the industry, and once we get those seeds planted, I’m a firm believer that they grow into educated community members who make educated decisions to bring community-minded data centers to their community.
